intro: The Mahamrityunjaya Mantra is a single verse addressed to Shiva, found in the Rigveda (7.59.12) and carried forward through centuries of oral and ritual use in Sanskrit worship. It is also called the Tryambakam mantra, after its opening word, which names Shiva as the three-eyed one. The verse speaks of fragrance, of nourishment and growth, and of release from bondage in the manner of a ripened cucumber falling free from its vine. It does not ask for wealth or victory; its language is about health, steadiness, and freedom from the fear that surrounds death. Across generations it has been used in daily worship, in healing contexts, and at moments of transition in a person's life. This page sets out what the verse contains, how it is traditionally recited, and what the tradition says it is for, without claiming any particular result for the reader.

groups.heading: Invocation: Tryambakam, the three-eyed one
groups.body: The mantra opens by naming Shiva as Tryambaka, the one with three eyes, and offering worship to him in that form. This opening line is an act of address rather than a request — it simply names the deity being approached before anything is asked. In the wider tradition, the three eyes are read as sun, moon and fire, or as the faculties of seeing past, present and future. The line sets the tone for the rest of the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra: before anything is asked for, the one being worshipped is identified and honoured.

groups.heading: Sugandhim: the fragrant one
groups.body: The next word describes Shiva as sugandhim, fragrant. Commentators have long read this as pointing to something beyond literal scent — a quality of wholeness or well-being that spreads outward, the way a pleasant fragrance fills a space without effort. In the context of the verse, this fragrance is linked to the nourishing, sustaining aspect of the deity being invoked, setting up the next phrase about growth and sustenance.

groups.heading: Pushtivardhanam: one who nourishes and increases
groups.body: This phrase calls Shiva the one who nourishes and causes growth — pushti meaning nourishment or abundance, vardhana meaning increase. Read alongside the previous line, the verse is building a picture of a deity associated with sustenance and flourishing, not only with dissolution, which is the role more commonly attached to Shiva in other contexts. This pairing of fragrance and nourishment forms the first half of the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra, establishing the quality being sought before the verse turns to its central image.

groups.heading: Urvarukamiva bandhanan: the image of the cucumber
groups.body: Here the verse introduces its central simile: urvarukam, a cucumber or gourd, iva, like, bandhanan, from its bondage or attachment. The image is of a ripe fruit loosening naturally from the vine it has grown on — not torn away, but released in its own time because it has reached ripeness. This comparison is the structural heart of the mantra, and everything before and after it is built around this single picture of natural, unforced release.

groups.heading: Mrityor mukshiya: release from death
groups.body: This phrase asks for release — mukshiya, may I be freed — from mrityoh, death or the condition of mortality. Paired with the cucumber image, the request is not phrased as an escape or a tearing away but as the same kind of natural loosening the fruit undergoes when ripe. This is the verse's central petition within the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra, and it is usually read as addressing the fear and bondage associated with death rather than death as a biological event alone.

groups.heading: Ma amritat: not from immortality
groups.body: The closing phrase, ma amritat, is usually read as 'not from immortality' — that is, the release sought is from death's grip, not a severing from the deathless or eternal. Traditional commentators read this final phrase as balancing the previous line: the verse does not ask to be cut off from everything, only to be freed from the particular bondage of fear and mortality, while remaining connected to what is lasting. This closes the single verse that makes up the entire Mahamrityunjaya Mantra.

recitation: The Mahamrityunjaya Mantra is recited both as part of regular worship and at particular moments considered significant by tradition. Monday, associated with Shiva, is commonly treated as a favourable day for its recitation, as are the lunar day of Pradosha and the festival of Mahashivratri. It is also recited during illness, before surgery, at times of fear or uncertainty, and in daily sandhya or puja practice by those who have taken it up as a personal discipline. A common method is japa — repeating the verse a fixed number of times, often in multiples of 108, using a mala (prayer beads) to keep count, though the specific number varies by family and teacher. Some traditions prescribe a longer practice, such as reciting it across many days during Shravan or other auspicious periods. It may be chanted aloud in a group, as in temple settings, or silently as personal practice. Before beginning, many people perform a short invocation or offer water, flowers, or a lit lamp to an image of Shiva. The pace of recitation is generally slow and clear rather than rushed, since the verse is short and its sound is considered as important as its sense. None of these customs are fixed rules; they vary across regions, lineages and individual teachers.
tradition: Within the tradition, the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra is held to be connected with health, steadiness of mind, and the easing of fear around death and illness — themes that follow directly from its own language of fragrance, nourishment and release. Ayurvedic and temple traditions have long associated it with recovery from sickness, and it is frequently included in healing rites and prayers offered on behalf of someone who is unwell. Teachers across different lineages describe its purpose differently — some emphasise protection, some emphasise inner calm, some read it primarily as a meditation on impermanence using the cucumber image as its anchor. What is consistently said, across these varied readings, is that the verse is addressed to Shiva in his sustaining aspect, and that its content is about release rather than acquisition. This page reports these attributions as they are held within the tradition, without asserting that recitation produces any specific outcome for anyone reciting it.

faq.a: It roughly translates to 'victory over death,' though the verse itself does not use those exact words. It comes from an address to Shiva as the fragrant, nourishing one, followed by a request to be released from death's bondage the way a ripe fruit loosens from its vine, while remaining connected to what is lasting.

faq.q: Who can recite the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra?
faq.a: Traditionally it has been recited by anyone who wishes to, though some lineages recommend learning the pronunciation from a teacher first, since it is in Sanskrit and the sound is considered important. It is used by individuals in personal practice as well as in group or temple settings.

faq.q: Is there a fixed number of times it should be chanted?
faq.a: Custom varies. A common practice is repetition in multiples of 108 using a mala, but some traditions prescribe other counts or durations, such as a set number of days. There is no single rule followed everywhere; the number is generally decided by the practitioner's own teacher or family custom.

faq.q: Is the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra only chanted during illness?
faq.a: No. While it is often recited during illness or before medical procedures, it is also part of regular daily worship for many people, and is chanted on days like Monday and during Mahashivratri regardless of health concerns.

faq.q: Does chanting this mantra guarantee a particular outcome?
faq.a: This page does not claim that. The tradition associates the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra with themes of steadiness, health and release from fear, and describes customary occasions for its use, but it does not promise specific results, and this explanation avoids making such claims.
